name: Edmund Burke
role: Anglo-Irish statesman, MP and political thinker (1729–1797)
summary: Burke defended the British balanced constitution, an established church, hereditary rank and the security of property, and argued that society is a partnership of the living, the dead and the unborn. He favoured gradual repair over abstract rights, opposed pure democracy and the French Revolution, and backed free commerce, Catholic relief, Irish trade and the impeachment of Warren Hastings for arbitrary power.

gradual-change.rationale: In the Reflections he sets 'a disposition to preserve, and an ability to improve' as his standard of a statesman and says a state without means of some change lacks the means of its conservation.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: The Reflections require change to respect inherited institutions and to proceed by repair, never by subversion; the state is approached 'as to the wounds of a father'.

generational-constitutional-review.rationale: The Reflections reject the idea that each generation may remake the constitution: those living may not 'cut off the entail or commit waste on the inheritance'.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: In the Reflections the living are life-renters bound to ancestors and posterity, with no right to change the state at pleasure.

sacred-nation.rationale: The Reflections say the commonwealth is 'consecrated' and a partnership between the living, the dead and the unborn.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: The Reflections and the 1782 speech present the constitution and nation as an inheritance continuous over ages, a prescriptive 'election of ages'.

separate-church-state.rationale: Burke calls the Church Establishment the first of English prejudices and says the state must be consecrated by a state religious establishment.

national-church-status.rationale: He resolves to keep 'an established church' and defends the Protestant establishment and its revenues in the Reflections.

more-religion-public.rationale: Religion is 'the basis of civil society' and a state religion is necessary to awe those holding power (Reflections).

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Rulers act 'in the person of God' and the Hastings speech says 'all power is of God'.

religion-illusion.rationale: Burke holds man is 'by his constitution a religious animal' and religion the source of all comfort, which contradicts treating it as illusory comfort (Reflections).

dynastic-succession.rationale: The Reflections defend hereditary succession to the crown as the settled principle of the constitution.

elective-rulers.rationale: The Reflections reject a 'right to choose our own governors' and defend the crown as hereditary rather than elected.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: He defends an established hereditary monarchy within a balanced constitution, and calls a reformed, balanced monarchy the best government for a great country.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He defends the hereditary House of Peers and hereditary distinction as the ballast of the commonwealth (Reflections).

mixed-constitution.rationale: He resolves to keep 'an established monarchy, an established aristocracy, and an established democracy, each in the degree it exists'.

second-chamber.rationale: He describes the hereditary House of Peers as the third of the legislature and defends it against abolition.

natural-rulers.rationale: The Appeal defends a 'natural aristocracy, without which there is no nation', and the Reflections place government in virtue and wisdom, 'not indifferently to every man'.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: The Reflections say no rotation or appointment by lot can generally be good in government.

democracy-best.rationale: He calls a perfect democracy 'the most shameless thing in the world' and says popular will is not the standard of right.

direct-votes.rationale: His condemnation of pure democracy and rejection of binding popular mandates tells against deciding laws by direct vote.

single-common-good.rationale: In the Bristol speech Parliament is a deliberative assembly of one nation with one interest, the general good, not local purposes or hostile interests.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The encyclopedia presents parliamentary sovereignty as the basis of stable government in his thought.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Reflections deny a right to choose governors and favour inherited prescription, while the Tract on the Popery Laws says a law needs at least implied consent of those bound.

revolution-justified.rationale: Revolution is 'the very last resource', justified by grave necessity as in 1688, so he does not hold it is never justified.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: He defends 1688 as a necessary act against a king who subverted the fundamental laws, while denying a general right to cashier rulers for misconduct.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The 1782 speech rejects making a constitution on a theory by popular claim of right and defends prescription over choice.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: In the Hastings impeachment: 'Law and arbitrary power are in eternal enmity'; arbitrary power is blasphemy in religion.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The Hastings speech insists that power exists under law and that judges are bound by it.

universal-morality.rationale: He declares that 'the laws of morality are the same everywhere' and rejects 'geographical morality'.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: The Tract says a law against equity is void: laws are only declaratory of original justice and cannot bind against the higher law.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The Tract denies that 'the black-letter and the king's arms' make law; legal form alone confers no authority.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: 'All men have equal rights; but not to equal things': equal right to justice and to the fruits of industry (Reflections), echoed in the Tract on equal justice.

equal-outcomes.rationale: 'Those who attempt to level never equalize'; he denies a right to an equal dividend (Reflections).

property-fundamental.rationale: He condemns the confiscation of Church property and says no one may seize the goods of an unoffending citizen on any pretext of public service.

land-redistribution.rationale: He condemns forced seizure of estates by whole descriptions of owners as tyranny and rapine.

tax-inheritance.rationale: He calls the power of perpetuating property in families among the most valuable features of property.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: He treats great masses of property as the 'ballast' and natural rampart of the commonwealth.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: 'The market settles, and alone can settle, that price'; government cannot supply the poor what commerce withholds (Scarcity).

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Scarcity opposes fixing grain prices by authority and says arbitrary regulation lays an axe to the root of production.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Labour is a commodity subject to the laws of trade, and wages should not be raised by authority (Scarcity).

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: He urges resisting the idea that it is within the competence of government to supply the poor with necessaries.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Relief belongs to the 'jurisdiction of mercy' where the magistrate has no place, and charity is left to private discretion (Scarcity).

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Charity to the poor is called 'a direct and obligatory duty upon all Christians' (Scarcity).

free-trade.rationale: His Irish trade letters argue that England and Ireland may flourish together and that trade is not a limited thing; he urged a free trade in all ports of the isles.

non-intervention.rationale: Remarks on the Policy of the Allies hold that interference in another country is always a right where charity or safety call for it.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: He opposed the 1777 partial suspension of Habeas Corpus as subverting the principle of liberty and justice.

traditional-family.rationale: He says public affections begin in families and the little platoon, and condemns reducing marriage to concubinage.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: He remarks that divorce is happily no regular head of registry among civilized nations and condemns the Jacobin divorce rate.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The Reflections defend inherited manners, religion and institutions as a national inheritance.

notes: Themes searched in the texts: economy, government, society, world, liberty, means, culture. Ecology, technology and most modern statements (healthcare, gender, drugs, environment) have no position in his writings and stay null. The Vindication of Natural Society is a satire he later disowned and is not used.
